content: Epigaea repens, commonly known as Mayflower or Trailing Arbutus, is a low-growing, spreading shrub that belongs to the Ericaceae family. This plant is native to a wide range of regions, including areas from Newfoundland to Florida, extending westward to Kentucky and the Northwest Territory. It is also found in certain parts of Central Europe and Western Africa. The flowers of Epigaea repens are pink in color, gradually fading to nearly white as they mature. They are highly fragrant and measure approximately 1/2 inch in diameter when fully expanded. These flowers are arranged in clusters, which can vary in number, and are located at the terminal ends of the branches. The calyx consists of five dry, overlapping sepals, while the corolla is salver-shaped, featuring a slender, hairy tube that flares out into five equal lobes. The plant has ten stamens and a single pistil, which is characterized by a column-like style and a stigma divided into five lobes. The stem of this plant spreads along the ground, as suggested by its genus name Epigaea, which means on the earth. The stems are woody, and the leafy twigs are covered with rusty-colored hairs. The leaves are alternately arranged, oval in shape, and rounded at the base. The upper surface of the leaves is smooth, while the underside is more or less hairy. These leaves are evergreen, weather-worn, and attached to the stem by short, rusty, hairy petioles. Epigaea repens is a slow-growing plant that thrives in moist, acidic soils rich in humus. It prefers shaded environments for optimal growth. This species holds cultural significance as it is the floral emblem of both Massachusetts and Nova Scotia.
